2. Brief facts giving rise to the present petition as contended by the petitioners are as follows:-
The petitioners claimed to be the owners of the subject lands situated across Sy.no.133/1, 133/2 and 133/3 133/5 and 133/6 of Doddatoguru village and Sy.No.41/1 of chikkatoguru village, Begur hobli, Bangalore south taluk, totally measuring an extent of 10 acres 12 guntas described as Schedule A,B, C and properties.
It is contended that the 1st respondent is the State of Karnataka while respondents 2 and 3 are the KIADB and the SALO, KIADB.
The 4th respondent claims to be an allottee of the subject lands of the schedule properties from the KIADB and respondent No.5 is the Managing Director of 4th respondent - company.

2.1 On 12.05.2004, the Notification under Section 3(1), 1(3) and 28(1) of the KIAD Act were issued in respect of the schedule properties, pursuant to which, a final notification under Section 28(4) was issued by the respondents 1 to 3.

The petitioners challenged the said Notifications in W.P.No.10828/2012 which was disposed off on 31.08.2012 by the learned Single Judge who was pleased to quash the final K. Gajendran vs The State Of Karnataka on 15 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/70615664/
8 notification dated 28.10.2004 and remit the matter back to the respondents 1 to 3 for reconsideration afresh in accordance with law after providing an opportunity to both the petitioners herein as well as respondents 4 and 5 herein.

sentences.text: 2.2 Subsequently, the SLAO passed an order dated 05.07.2013 under Section 28(3) of the KIAD Act rejecting the objection / claim of the petitioners and recommended issuance of the final notification, pursuant to which, the 2nd respondent issued a final notification dated 16.11.2017 under Section 28(4) of the KIAD Act.

Thus,
aggrieved by the impugned Notifications, petitioners are before this Court by way of the present petition.

3. The petition is opposed by the respondents by filing separate statement of objections and documents inter alia contending that apart from the fact that the petitioners do not have locus- standi to file the present petition, also do not have any manner of right, title, interest or possession over the schedule properties.

The respondents supported the impugned acquisition proceedings as well as allotment of the schedule properties in favour of respondents 4 and 5 and contended that there is no merit in the petition and that the same is liable to be dismissed.

4. Heard Sri.Reuben Jacob, learned Senior counsel for the petitioners and Sri.S.S.Naganand,
learned Senior counsel for respondents 4 and 5 as well as Sri.Vijaykumar A.Patil, learned counsel for the respondents - KIADB and learned AGA for the State and perused the material on record.
5.

In addition to reiterating the various contentions urged in the petition and referring to the material on record, learned Senior counsel for the petitioners submitted that the impugned acquisition proceedings are vitiated by fraud, since the power of eminent domain has been exercised by in order to favour 5th respondent to overcome its defective title to the Schedule-A, B & C properties and the power of eminent domain in the instant case is a colourable exercise of power and amounts to fraud on power as the State machinery has been misused by 5th respondent in order to overcome the bogus sale deeds set up by him to claim title to the Schedule-A, B & C properties.

It was submitted that the SLAO was required to consider the objections of the petitioner in view of the earlier order of this Hon'ble Court in W.P.No.10828/2012 and pass a reasoned and speaking order after providing opportunity to the petitioners which has not been done in the instant case.
It was therefore submitted that the impugned notifications deserve to be quashed.

sentences.text: I have given my anxious consideration to the rival submissions and perused the material on record.

8. A perusal of the material on record including the rival contentions will indicate that the petitioners have already approached the competent civil court in O.S.No.1102/2012 in relation to the petition schedule properties which are the subject matters of the present petition.
In the said suit, the respondents 4 and 5 are arrayed as defendant No.7 and defendant No.14 and the KIADB as defendant No.15.
There are other defendants also in the said suit including the family members of the respondent No.4.
It is an undisputed fact that the said suit is being contested by the defendants.
9. A perusal of the plaint schedule properties involved in the said suit will indicate that the same are also the subject matter of the present petition.

sentences.text: 12. As can be seen from the aforesaid order dated 22.03.2021 passed by this Court, the present petition was directed to be re-listed after disposal of R.A.No.57/2020 by the 1st appellate court.

13. Subsequently, the said R.A.No.57/2020 was disposed of by the 1st appellate court vide judgment and decree dated 29.01.2022, whereby the 1st appellate court set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and remitted the matter back to the trial court for reconsideration afresh in accordance with law after providing an opportunity to both parties to adduce oral and documentary evidence.

As stated earlier, in the first instance, the plaint was rejected and the suit was dismissed under Order 7 Rule 11 CPC without recording evidence and the 1st appellate court has come to the conclusion that the mixed questions of fact and law including the dispute regarding title and possession between the petitioners and respondents were involved in respect of the schedule properties which would have to be adjudicated upon only after a full fledged trial and

consequently,
the 1st appellate court remitted the matter back to the trial court for reconsideration afresh in accordance with law.

The operative portion of the 1st appellate court reads as under:-
"
The appeal filed by the appellants U/s 96 of CPC is hereby allowed.

The matter is remanded back to learned trial Court for fresh consideration by giving opportunity to both parties to lead their evidence and decide this case in accordance with law on merits without any prejudice of this order.

Office is hereby directed to send back the entire records along with copy of this judgment to the trial Court for reference."
14.
Though the respondents 4 and 5 challenged the said order passed in R.A.No.57/2020, by preferring MSA No. 45/2022, the same was dismissed by this Court vide order dated 03.02.2023.

sentences.text: 15. Subsequent to remand, the suit in O.S.No.1102/2012 is still pending before the trial court and presently stands posted to 21.03.2023 for appearance of the parties.

16. As stated supra, the material on record including the rival claims and contentions between the petitioners and the respondents as well as the other parties towards O.S.No.1102/2012 will clearly indicate that there are several contentious issues and disputed / complicated questions of title of law and fact as well as rival claims to title and possession over the schedule properties which are seized by the competent civil court in the said suit filed by the petitioners herein seeking comprehensive relief.

It cannot be gainsaid that the said disputed questions of fact are incapable of being adjudicated by this Court in the present petition, more particularly when the same are seized by the competent civil court in O.S.No.1102/2012 referred to supra.

Under these circumstances, I am of the considered opinion that the present challenge to the acquisition proceedings at the instance of the petitioners cannot be considered at this stage prior to disposal of O.S.No.1102/2012 by the competent civil court.

To the extent whether the petitioners would have a right as against the claim of respondent no.3 or respondent no.4, is therefore, subject to the decision of the civil court in the pending civil suit.

It is also brought on record that insofar as the acquisition having been completed and compensation amount having been deposited in court, is locked up in dispute as between the respondent no.4 and the erstwhile owners and the further lease deed executed in favour of the third respondent
is also seriously disputed by the KIADB and the same is subject matter of a pending writ petition filed by respondent no.3 in WP 33950/2011 before this court.

In that background, the fact that the first petitioner was a witness in a civil suit between the fourth respondent and the erstwhile owners of the land would lead to a presumption that they are not absolute strangers, in that, respondent no.4 was acquainted with petitioner no.1.

The fact that the lands have been sold either as agricultural lands or as sites formed out of agricultural land and thereby having succeeded in two transactions having taken place in respect of the same properties, is again a question of fact which is to be adjudicated in the civil suit.

In a disputed matter such as this, to proceed on the basis that the bona fides of the parties is above board and to permit acquisition proceedings to reach finality is not welcome and as regards which, this court cannot be a mute witness to the disputed transaction as between the parties.

The fact that the respondent no.4 has offered the entire lands purchased by him to be acquired voluntarily and thereafter funnelled back to respondent no.3, of which he is the Managing Director, which according to the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioners is itself a suspicious transaction, which should have put the KIADB on guard as to the bona fides of the said respondent, is not a circumstance that can be readily accepted.
But given the attendant circumstances, it is certainly an aspect to be addressed.

In that view of the matter, if in order, the notification under Section 28(4) of the KIADB Act to be sustained as being without any blemish, it would be necessary for the KIADB to be aware of the other circumstance which may or which may not have been brought to its attention, especially, in the light of the circumstance that the KIADB itself disputes the lease deed under which the third respondent is now claiming.

Therefore,
it is in the fitness of things that the matter be remitted for a fresh consideration, after affording an opportunity to the parties to have their say notwithstanding the long lapse of time and even possible knowledge on the part of the petitioners of any acquisition proceedings.
For if this objection as to delay and laches is permitted, if it has the effect of respondent no.4 seeking advantage thereof, it cannot be a ground for turning the petitioners out.

Therefore, it would be in the interest of justice and in the fitness of things, to permit the KIADB to hold a fresh hearing under Section 28(3) of the KIADB Act and to take further steps thereafter in accordance with law.

The fact that the lands have been sold either as agricultural lands or as sites formed out of agricultural land and thereby having succeeded in two transactions having taken place in respect of the same properties, is again a question of fact which is to be adjudicated in the civil suit.
In a disputed matter such as this, to proceed on the basis that the bona fides of the parties is above board and to permit acquisition proceedings to reach finality is not welcome and as regards which, this court cannot be a mute witness to the disputed transaction as between the parties.
The fact that the respondent no.4 has offered the entire lands purchased by him to be acquired voluntarily and thereafter funnelled back to respondent no.3, of which he is the Managing Director, which according to the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioners is itself a suspicious transaction, which should have put the KIADB on guard as to the bona fides of the said respondent, is not a circumstance that can be readily accepted.
Therefore,
it is in the fitness of things that the matter be remitted for a fresh consideration, after affording an opportunity to the parties to have their say notwithstanding the long lapse of time and even possible knowledge on the part of the petitioners of any acquisition proceedings.
For if this objection as to delay and laches is permitted, if it has the effect of respondent no.4 seeking advantage thereof, it cannot be a ground for turning the petitioners out.
Under these circumstances, merely because this Court set aside the final notification in W.P.No.10828/2012 and remitted the matter for reconsideration afresh, it cannot be said that the petitioners have locus standi or that the said order passed by this Court be made the basis to come to the conclusion that the petitioners have locus standi and consequently, even this contention of the petitioners cannot be accepted.
20.
g) In other words, if it is held that the petitioners have no right over the schedule properties, as a corollary, they would also have no locus standi to challenge/assail the impugned acquisition proceedings especially when they seek to agitate their alleged private rights and the present petition is not a public interest litigation;
h) Consequently, the legality and validity of the impugned acquisition notifications can be examined and adjudicated upon by this Court only after the proprietary and possessory rights of the parties are adjudicated upon and decided in the pending civil litigation and it cannot be said that at this stage that the petitioners have locus standi to maintain the present petition;
22. Insofar as the various other contentions and judgments relied upon by both sides are concerned,
as stated supra, since various contentious issues and disputed / complicated questions of title and possession as well as law and fact having been seized by the competent civil court, the said disputed questions are incapable of being adjudicated upon by this Court in the present petition.
